output:
A heat pump does not burn anything. It does not glow, and it does not make heat in the way a gas boiler or an electric heater does. Instead, it collects heat that already exists outside and brings it indoors.

That sounds impossible on a cold day, but cold air still contains plenty of heat. Even at freezing point, the air holds far more energy than you would guess. Heat only stops entirely at around minus 273°C. A heat pump simply needs something colder than the outside air to soak that warmth up.

So it uses a fluid called refrigerant, which boils at a startlingly low temperature. Outside, this fluid runs through coils with a fan blowing over them. The air feels cold to you, but it is warm compared with the refrigerant, so the fluid absorbs heat and turns to gas.

A compressor then squeezes that gas tightly. Squeezing makes it much hotter, hot enough to warm water for your radiators or air for your rooms. Having given up its heat indoors, the fluid cools, turns back to liquid, and heads outside to collect more.

Think of a sponge soaking up a thin film of water across a wide floor, then being wrung out into a single bucket. Nothing is created; it is gathered and concentrated.

This is why heat pumps beat ordinary electric heaters. A heater converts one unit of electricity into one unit of heat. A heat pump uses one unit of electricity to move three or four units of heat indoors. The electricity powers the pump, not the warmth itself.

The trade-off is temperature. Heat pumps deliver gentler, steadier warmth than a boiler, so they work best in well-insulated homes with large radiators or underfloor pipes.

In short, a heat pump is a fridge running in reverse, scavenging warmth from the outdoors and concentrating it inside your home.
